docs.title: Submission Details
docs.text:
Full Team Number: 9776C

Brief description of the novel aspect of the team's design:

Our team developed a dual-chamber color sorting system using a V-shaped sorter mechanism driven by a cam-actuated rotation system. Unlike traditional color sorting approaches that eject the wrong color, our design physically separates and stores both red and blue blocks in independent chambers. This enables strategic advantages in both match play (flexibility) and skills challenges (maximizing control zone scores). The system uses an optical sensor with queued-block processing, a 1:2 geared motor (5.5W), and a cam-driven standoff pivot mechanism that can rotate ±120° to direct blocks into either chamber. The design includes a 6-state state machine for reliable sorting without jamming.

docs.title: Identify the page numbers and/or the section(s) where documentation of the development of this aspect can be found:
docs.text:
Primary Documentation: - Color Sorting System - Main Page - Complete design process from Identify through implementation - Intake System - Integration with intake mechanism and decision matrix - Scoring Architecture - How color sorting integrates with dual-chamber lever design

Key sections within Color Sorting documentation: - Brainstorm: Comparison of 4 different sorting approaches (Horizontal Plus, V-sorter, Top Flex Wheels, Back Flex Wheels) with detailed diagrams - Select: Weighted decision matrix with criteria including size, compatibility, consistency, and lever interference avoidance (V-sorter scored 314 points vs. next best at 210) - Implement/Design: Two complete design iterations showing mechanical refinement, sensor placement analysis, and motor/gearing calculations - Identify/Brainstorm/Select: Advanced physics analysis including sensor refresh rate constraints, motor inertia calculations, RPM requirements, and torque budgeting - System Latency Budget: Complete timing analysis showing 90ms total latency with queued-block architecture

docs.title: Explain why your submission is unique from other approaches to the problem it solves or task it performs:
docs.text:
Problem: Maximize autonomous and driver-control scoring in both match and skills challenges while maintaining speed and reliability.

Standard Industry Approach: Most competitive VEX bots use single-color ejection at the intake—if the wrong color is picked up, it's immediately ejected back. This prevents opponent scoring but wastes time and limits strategic flexibility.

Our Unique Solution: 1. Dual-Chamber Architecture: We physically separate colors into two independent 5-block chambers instead of ejecting, providing storage capacity and strategic control.

  1. Queued-Block Sensing: Instead of fly-by color detection (which requires split-second timing), our blocks physically queue at the sorter entrance. The optical sensor can take multiple confident reads on a stationary target, eliminating timing pressure and false positives.

  2. Cam-Driven Rotation: Our V-sorter uses a cam actuator with standoff push points and a collar-based pivot, a unique mechanical approach we designed through iterative refinement. This avoids the complexity of hinge abominations and provides consistent, reliable rotation without tolerance stack-up.

  3. Skills Challenge Advantage: By storing both colors, we can fill control zones with single-color blocks much more efficiently than competitors, directly addressing the skills challenge scoring rules that reward color-matched control zones (30 points total if achieved perfectly).

  4. Mathematical Foundation: Our design is backed by detailed calculations: motor inertia analysis (2.74×10⁻⁵ kg·m²), sensor timing budgets (100ms refresh with multiple reads), RPM requirements (267 RPM for 150ms block interval), and torque analysis (2.3 lb-in at 1:2 gearing).

Result: A system that is faster than manual color separation, more reliable than high-speed fly-by sensing, and strategically superior to single-color ejection systems. This approach is not commonly documented in VEX literature and represents original engineering innovation tailored to our specific competition strategy.

docs.text: Building off of the previous page, we can go to various competitions, and see all of these strategies implemented to other's bots, as well as our own.

docs.title: Score fast:
docs.text: This is essentially the main focus everyone does. Scoring the most points is how games are won, so it makes sense. A lot of strategy depended on scoring and de-scoring. The biggest part was the long goals, which were worth a lot of points. Scoring and de-scoring here is where almost all the bots focused on.

docs.title: Bully:
docs.text: Preventing the other bots from doing anything was very successful for us. It prevents them from scoring and de-scoring, basically disabling their robot. It's allowed in the rules, however we can't hold them, just repeatedly bump into them.

docs.title: Camping:
docs.text: Scoring a whole section, and then guard it. It is a winning strategy, but it isn't very fun. Another team did this against us, and we didn't know how to deal with it. It's a strategy to think about.

docs.title: Score points where others can't:
docs.text: This strategy loses its value the farther into the season we get. As more teams develop their bot, they all eventually are able to score everywhere.

docs.title: Identify:
docs.text: When new systems are added to a bot, the code must be edited. One common approach to handle adding a new button input to the code is to simply add a new button check and compare. This works and there is not much wrong with this approach, It gets the job done. However, it has some small drawbacks if you use more advanced types of input. The main drawback is that it makes your code very messy. This makes it hard to find problems or make changes quickly. It also makes harder for anyone else to understand what your code does. Another drawback is that it is repetitive. Code for a new button is often very similar to one of the other buttons; the only difference is usually just checking from a different button. Make your code DRY, not WET. This is one of the greatest principles that all programmers should strive for. DRY code is code in which you D - Don't R - Repeat Y - Yourself. Opposed to WET code, in which you W - Write E - Everything T - Twice.

docs.title: Brainstorm:
docs.text: To make the code cleaner and drier, we are going to use 2 files separate from main.cpp, buttonState.h and buttonState.cpp. The .h, or header file, will be essentially be a clean "list" of functions and variables to be found in the .cpp, or source file. The source file will have the the actual logic. There are many ways to use these files to accomplish our button related tasks. Some of the ways I can think of are:

docs.title: Plain functions:
docs.text:
This would be very simple; every button type would have their own function. Every cycle of the code for every button we would call something like: 

// call an update function that uses the current and prevous button state
bool a_ouptut = updateToggleHoldButton(previousBtnState, 
controller1.get_analog(pros::E_CONTROLLER_DIGITAL_A)); 

// update the last state for next loop
bool previousBtnState = controller1.get_analog(pros::E_CONTROLLER_DIGITAL_A)
// and possibly other variables nessesary for this calculation.


// or, for another button type:
// almost the same as before, but with a different function. 
bool b_ouptut = updateToggleButton(previousBtnState, 
controller1.get_analog(pros::E_CONTROLLER_DIGITAL_B)); 

bool previousBtnState = controller1.get_analog(pros::E_CONTROLLER_DIGITAL_B)
Then in our header and source files we would define logic for each of those button types. While this is definitely cleaner than rewriting the same logic over and over again, it is far from as clean as it can get.

docs.title: Function selector:
docs.text:
Instead of using different functions, we could instead group all of the logic together into a singular function. We would then use a "button type" variable to identify what parts of the logic are relevant to the button. We additionally could use this Identifier to keep track of the variables needed for the calculation. This would look something like: 

// in an initialization funtion or in the global scope:
// define a new button
Button intakeButton(ButtonType::TOGGLE_HOLD); // and give it a button type.

// then later, in the loop:

bool isIntakeActive =
    intakeButton.update(controller1.get_analog(pros::E_CONTROLLER_DIGITAL_Y))


// and in the header and source:

// a button types list:
enum class ButtonType {
    HOLD,        
    TOGGLE,       
    TOGGLE_HOLD   
};

// a constructor to interpret what type of button it is 
ButtonState(ButtonType t) : type(t) {}

// and any other variables needed 
    ButtonType type;
    bool curr = false;
    bool prev = false;
    int heldMs = 0;

// then all the calculations in the update function.
bool update(bool input) {
    // logic goes here
}
This is almost exactly what we did for our last bot, but I feel like I can do a little better.

docs.title: Everything in the new file:
docs.text: This builds on the previous version, with a few changes. The logic for these button types needs to be run every cycle. The last 2 version did that by always running an update function for every button. We can instead create a dedicated update all buttons function. Last 2 versions also used controller1.get_analog(pros::E_CONTROLLER_DIGITAL_A) to update the button; we can move this into the external code as well. We would then add a read button output function.

docs.title: Select:
docs.text: I am going to implement the last idea I explained as it leaves the main code very clean.

docs.title: Implement:
docs.text: To start, I made enum class "ButtonType" that defined the button types. Then I made 2 classes: Input and InputGroup. The InputGroup allows me to manage all of the buttons in a group. This is handy if we ever want to use a second controller or have multiple different button layouts in the same code. It has a constructor InputGroup(pros::Controller &controller) : controller(controller) {} this lets us set what controller to read the button inputs from. It also has void addButton(), void updateAll(), and bool getState().

docs.title: Adding a button:
docs.text:
Adding a button takes 3 arguments: the name of the new input, and a list (done with a vector) of one or more buttons to use as the input, and what button type it is. For example: 

// add a new button with a name, input(s), and a button type.
void InputGroup::addButton(std::string name, 
                           std::vector<pros::controller_digital_e_t> 
                           btns, ButtonType type)

When the function is called, it passes the list of buttons, the button type, and the controller to the Input constructor, creating a new "Input" object. stores the name and the new object in the unordered map, "buttons", like so: buttons.emplace(name, Input(controller, btns, type));

docs.title: Updating the buttons:
docs.text:
Running myInputGroup.updateAll() allows us to update all the inputs defined in the input group. The updateAll() function is simple. All it does is reads through the unordered map and runs the update function for each of them, like so: 

for (auto &[unused, input] : buttons) { // for each input part of the group,
    input.update();                     // run the update function.
}
The update function however, is not as simple. It is responsible for preparing the output for any of the 6 button types. It starts by updating the previous and current state variables for the button, like so: 
prev = curr;  // start by updating the previous state variable by coping
              // the current state variable.
curr = false; // reset the current state variable.
    

for (auto btn : buttons) { // then, for every button listed in the buttons vector:
    if (controller.get_digital(btn)) { // check if the button is pressed;
        curr = true; // if it is, set the current state variable to true
        break;       // and stop checking buttons.
    }
}
// if none of the buttons in the vector were pressed;
// the current state variable never changed from when we set it to false.
After determining the previous and current state of the buttons, It does more logic to determine other variables like rising edge or falling edge detection. This part is much more complicated, so I won't describe it in as much detail.

docs.title: First is the "if the button is currently pressed" logic:
docs.text:
if (curr) { // -------------- button is currently pressed -------------- //
    fallingEdge = false; // falling edge is never true if it is pressed
    if (!prev) { // - IS currently pressed and WASN'T prevously pressed - //
        risingEdge = true; // this is the only time rising edge is true
        heldMs = 0; // reset the held time as the button was just pressed
        toggleState = !toggleState; // toggle here so that holding the
                                    // button doesn't repetitively toggle
    } else { // ---- IS currently pressed and WAS prevously pressed ---- //
        risingEdge = false; // no rising edge if it was held previously
        heldMs += LOOP_MS;  // to track held time, add the loop time
    }

docs.title: Inside of the "if button is currently pressed" logic, there is also more logic to handle the most complex button type I have defined, specifically the toggle or hold button type:
docs.text:
// ------------- if our button is a toggle hold button ------------- //
if (buttonType == ButtonType::TOGGLE_HOLD &&
    heldMs >= toggleThresholdMs) {  // and it has been held long enough:
    if (InvertedTH) {               // if inverted toggling is on,
        toggleState = !toggleState; // invert the toggle from before
    } else {                        // if inverted toggling is off,
        toggleState = false;        // always cancel toggle state
    }
}
Having inverted toggling off means that if the state is toggled on and then we hold and release the button, it will turn off. This is fairly intuitive, but sometimes it is useful to have inverted toggling. If the toggled state is on, and then we hold and release the button, instead of resetting it to false, it will set it back to what it was before. For example, We could have a motor that spins when the input state is active. Then we press and release the button before the hold threshold, it toggles on, making the motor spin. if we then press and release the button before the threshold, it will immediately turn off, regardless of whether inverted toggling is on or not. However, if inverted toggling was on and we pressed the button then released it after the threshold, it would turn the motor back on after releasing the button.

docs.title: After that is the "if button is not currently pressed" logic:
docs.text:
} else { // -------------- button is NOT currently pressed -------------- //
    risingEdge = false; // rising edge is never true if it is not pressed
    heldMs = 0;         // the button is not held, so the held time is 0
    if (prev) { // - ISN'T currently pressed and WAS previously pressed - //
        fallingEdge = true; // this is the only time falling edge is true
    } else { // - ISN'T currently pressed and WASN'T prevoiusly pressed - //
        fallingEdge = false; // no falling edge if it wasn't held previously
    }
}
And that is all the logic for the 6 different types of buttons.

docs.title: Reading a button:
docs.text:
To read a button, we can run myInputGroup.getState("myInputsName"). The getState() function then looks through the unordered map from before for matching names, in this case, it is looking for "myInputName". It then looks at the object paired with that name, and runs the getOutput() function. The getOutput() function is very simple, it just returns a boolean based on which button type the input is: 

bool Input::getOutput() {
    switch (buttonType) {           // check what buttonType this input is
    case ButtonType::TOGGLE:        // if it is a toggle button,
        return toggleState;         // return the toggle state
    case ButtonType::HOLD:          // if it is a hold button,
        return curr;                // simply return the current state
    case ButtonType::TOGGLE_HOLD:   // if it is a toggle/hold button,
        return toggleState || curr; // return true if toggle or curr are true
    case ButtonType::RISING_EDGE:   // if it is a rising edge button,
        return risingEdge;          // return the rising edge state
    case ButtonType::FALLING_EDGE:  // if it is a falling edge button,
        return fallingEdge;         // return the falling edge state
    case ButtonType::RISING_FALLING_EDGE: // if it is a rising/falling edge,
        return risingEdge || fallingEdge; // return true if either are true
    default:                              // if it is SOMEHOW not a valid type,
        return curr;                      // return the raw state.
    }
}

Additionally, the getState() function can take one more argument; a boolean that dictates whether the return should be the raw data or should follow the button type structure. By default the raw flag is set to false, but if we instead set it to one, it simply returns the curr variable: 

bool InputGroup::getState(std::string name, bool raw) {
    if (!raw) { // check to see if we want the output to be raw or "normal"
        return buttons.at(name).getOutput(); // if normal, use the funtion.
    } else {                          // if the output should be raw,
        return buttons.at(name).curr; // instead return just the curr variable.
    }
}

docs.title: Why do we need to color sort?
docs.text:
Our bot's scoring and storage mechanism is 2 chambers. We chose to use 2 chambers because it has a few advantages over a regular, single chamber lever bot. One of these benefits is simply more storage space. The other main benefit, however, excites me more; having 2 separate chambers allows us to separate the red blocks from the blue blocks.

Any bot without a color sorting mechanism runs the risk of scoring points for the opponent and their options are limited to: avoid the wrong color as much as possible, carefully try to score their own color while trying to remove the opposing color, or just give up and score the opponent some points.

A bot with a color sorting system can simply pick up blocks and not worry about the bad ones. This saves a lot of time and does not score points for the opponent.

Not all lever bot designs that want to color sort need 2 barrels! In fact, I have not seen a single lever bot with 2 barrels, but I have seen plenty that can color sort. Most bots, lever or otherwise, simply eject the wrong color during or just after intaking. We considered this as well. Ignoring the benefit of increased storage, there is still another advantage our double chamber has over regular color sorting; The ability to keep the opposite color.

Why would we want to keep the wrong color? Perhaps we want to stop the other team from getting more blocks? No, It is too hard to monopolize blocks, too easy to descore, and 5-7 blocks wouldn't make much of a difference. Perhaps we want to use them to strategically position our blocks in the control zones? No, a single lever design that could adjust the block lineup would be better suited for that. Besides, that gives points to the other side, it is just as easy to pick up more of our own blocks. There appears to be no logical reason to want to hold on to your opponent's blocks in match! That is because there is not a good enough reason in a match to justify a double chamber design. The reason comes not from a match, but from the skills challenge.

This is the is scoring for the skills challenge:

Category Points Each Block Scored in a Goal 1 Point Each filled Control Zone in a Long Goal 5 Points Each filled Control Zone in a Center Goal 10 Points Each Cleared Park Zone 5 Points Each Cleared Loader 5 Points Parked Robot 15 Points There is 2 long goals and 2 center goals. That is 30 points for just the goals (not including the points for the individual blocks). The rule book explains these 2 categories as follows:

"A Control Zone is considered filled if it ends the Match containing its maximum number of Scored Blocks, and if all Blocks in that Control Zone are the same color (e.g., all are blue, or all are red). - i. In a Robot Skills Match, a Center Goal Control Zone must contain at least seven (7) Blocks to be considered filled. - ii. A Long Goal must include one or more of the following to be considered filled in a Robot Skills Match: 1. Three Blocks of the same color fully contained between the inner edges of the Control Zone tape lines. 2. Four Blocks of the same color fully contained between the outer edges of the Control Zone tape lines."

This means that in order to get these 30 points from control zones, all blocks in the control zone needs to be the same color. For a bot without color sorting, these 30 points are very difficult to get. With a regular color sorting bot, it becomes a little easier. But with our bot separates and keeps both colors, making this much easier. This allows us to in theory get very good skills scores, both autonomous and driver control.

docs.title: Speed Calculations (Revised With Physical Queue + Sensor Constraints)
Intake Speed Reality Check
docs.text:
At 70 in/s intake speed, treating blocks as spheres with diameter ~3.625 in:

\[ \text{Blocks/sec} = \frac{70\text{ in}}{\text{sec}} \cdot \frac{1\text{ block}}{3.625\text{ in}} = 19.3\text{ blocks/sec} \]

This tells us the intake speed is not the bottleneck.

Sorting reliability matters more than raw throughput.

Because blocks will physically queue at the sorter entrance if not processed fast enough, intake speed and sorting speed are decoupled. Once a block reaches the queue point, it effectively “waits,” removing the hard timing constraint that exists in fly-by sorting.

docs.title: Sorter Cycle Time Requirement
docs.text:
If blocks arrive every 150 ms (≈6.7 blocks/sec worst case), the sorter must complete a divert cycle within that window.

Required RPM for a 2/3 rotation cam move:

\[ \text{RPM} = \frac{2/3\text{ rotation}}{150\text{ ms}} \cdot \frac{1000}{1} \cdot \frac{60}{1} \approx 267\text{ RPM} \]

With 1:2 gearing, the 5.5W motor provides 400 RPM, giving ample margin even with conservative acceleration.

docs.title: Optical Sensor Refresh Reality
docs.text:
• Nominal refresh: ~100 ms
  • Effective polling (manual reads): 5–20 ms

Max reliable reads/sec (manual polling):

\[ \frac{1}{10\text{ ms}} = 100\text{ reads/sec} \]

However, without queuing, a block moving at 70 in/s would only be visible for:

\[ \frac{3.25\text{ in}}{70\text{ in/s}} = 46\text{ ms} \]

This is not enough to guarantee a read if the sensor refresh and block arrival are out of phase.

docs.title: Effect of Physical Queuing (Critical Change)
docs.text:
Because blocks physically stack and cannot enter the sort zone while another block is present:

  • The sensed block is stationary
  • The optical sensor can take multiple reads
  • Color confidence becomes deterministic rather than probabilistic

This eliminates the “missed block” failure mode entirely.

docs.title: Sensor Placement Constraints
docs.text:
• Space is extremely cramped
  • Max usable lead distance: ~3–4 inches
  • Distance sensor must share mounting location with optical sensor
  • Ambient light enters from the front and sides

docs.title: Ultra-Black Paint (Legality + Function)
docs.text:
Ultra-black paint (≈99.4% absorption):

  • Suppresses ambient lighting
  • Creates near-zero noise floor for brightness detection without much effort
  • Allows single-threshold triggering instead of averaging

Legality: Per R20a, materials used strictly as a color marker for a legal sensor are allowed. This qualifies.

Regular matte black (~95%) is acceptable if ultra-black is unavailable.

docs.title: Sensor Processing Logic (Queued Mode)
docs.text: Because the block is stationary while queued, the logic can be reactive instead of predictive.

docs.title: State Machine
docs.text:
• IDLE: Distance < threshold → block present
  • SENSE: Take 2–3 color reads (brightness wake-up)
  • ACTUATE: Snap cam to target (±120°)
  • READY: Hold cam, wait for intake pulse
  • RELEASE: Intake advances block into biased paddles
  • RESET: Wait until distance clears

docs.title: Brightness Threshold (Fast Path)
docs.text:
• Brightness < 10% → background
  • Brightness > 30% → block present

This avoids slow RGB math unless necessary.

docs.title: System Latency Budget (Reinterpreted)
docs.text:
Component Time Optical sensing (queued) 10–15 ms Code execution ~3 ms Motor acceleration ~2–3 ms Cam travel (1:2 gearing) ~75 ms Total (non-critical) ~90 ms

Because the block is waiting, this latency no longer needs to fit inside the travel time window.

docs.title: CAD-Derived Properties (Full Mechanism)
docs.text:
• Mass: 2.22 oz (63 g)
  • Center of mass nearly on axis
  • \(I_{zz} = 1.498\ \text{oz·in}^2\)

docs.title: Acceleration Reality
docs.text:
Converted inertia: $$ I_{zz} = 2.74 \times 10^{-5} \text{kg·m}^2 $$

The 5.5W motor can spin this mass to speed in ~2–3 ms. Acceleration is negligible; RPM is the true limiter.

docs.title: Gearing Comparison (Final)
docs.text: Gearing Torque @ Cam 180° Time Required Lead 1:1 1.55 lbs 150 ms ~10.5" 1:2 0.77 lbs 75 ms ~5" 1:3 0.5 lbs 50 ms ~3.5"

docs.title: Final Selection: 1:2 Gearing
docs.text:
• Enough torque to push against queued blocks
  • Fast enough to feel “instant”
  • Safest balance for a 5.5W motor

1:3 is rejected due to stall risk under spring load.

docs.title: Spring and Cam Design Implications
docs.text:
• The motor is fighting springs, not inertia
  • Add flat spots at cam peaks to prevent back-drive
  • Neutral cam position holds paddles open for easy entry

docs.title: Force Budget @ 1:2
docs.text:
• Torque: 2.3 lb-in
  • Lever arm: 3"
  • Available force: 0.77 lbs

Action item: If paddle movement requires >0.5 lbs, springs must be softened.

docs.title: Failure Recovery Logic
docs.text:
• If motor current spikes >2.0A:
  • Briefly reverse cam 20°
  • Retry snap
  • If color confidence fails after 5 reads:
  • Default to safe path (dump or majority color)

docs.title: Select:
docs.text: After revisiting mechanical feasibility, sensor reliability, timing constraints, and integration with the intake, the following selections are finalized for the color sorting system.

docs.title: Rotation and Actuation
docs.text:
• Actuation Method: Cam-driven rotation using standoff push points
  • Pivot Style: Collar-based central pivot
  • Material Choice: Steel V-walls for stiffness and repeatable geometry

This combination eliminates sliding-slot wear, reduces tolerance stackup, and allows the cam and pivot to share a common axis.

docs.title: Motor and Gearing
docs.text:
• Motor: 5.5W VEX motor
  • Gearing: **1:2 reduction

Justification:

  • Provides sufficient torque margin against spring load and queued blocks
  • Achieves sub-100 ms actuation without approaching stall conditions
  • Best balance of speed, reliability, and mechanical forgiveness

docs.title: Sensor Placement
docs.text:
Due to space constraints, the sensor can only either look at the floor ~3 inches ahead or at the cam walls ~0.5–1 inch away (painted with ~99.5% light-absorbing black).

Selected: cam-wall–referenced sensing

Looking at the cam walls provides a controlled, ultra-dark reference surface, giving far higher contrast and repeatability than floor sensing. Because blocks physically queue and remain stationary, the system can take multiple reads.

This design intentionally prioritizes accuracy over speed. With queued blocks, sorting does not need to happen in a fly-by window, allowing slower, higher-confidence sensing without impacting throughput.

Floor-looking sensing is therefore rejected due to inconsistent lighting and weaker color confidence.

docs.title: Identify:
docs.text: In Push Back, blocks scored in goals can be pushed back out by the opposing alliance. This means we need a way to descore opponent blocks from goals. Without a descoring mechanism, we're relying entirely on outscoring the opponent, which isn't always possible if they have a faster cycle time or a better autonomous.

docs.title: Goals:
docs.text:
• Be able to push opponent blocks out of goals
  • Keep the mechanism simple and lightweight so it doesn't interfere with our scoring or intake systems
  • Be able to deploy and retract quickly

docs.title: Constraints:
docs.text:
• Must fit within our overall size limits
  • Needs to go above the long goal so it can go above the middle part and not get obliterated
  • Must be able to hover in the block pushing state so it doesn't have to be in the goal when deployed.
  • Must fit below the long goal when the chamber is in the down position so it doesn't interfere with normal scoring operations

docs.title: Brainstorm:
docs.text:
We looked at two main ways to make the wing move:

  1. 4-bar linkage A parallel linkage that keeps the wing at a consistent angle as it deploys. More complex, takes up more space, but gives you precise control over the wing path.

  2. Simple pivot The wing is mounted on a single pivot point and swings out. Much more compact and fewer parts, but the wing traces an arc rather than a straight path.

docs.title: Select:
docs.text:
We went with the simple pivot because it's the most compact option and we're already tight on space. The key insight is that we can take advantage of the chamber's existing 4-bar linkage to make this work. When the chamber is in the up position, the pivot engages a one-way catch that holds the wing out in the deployed position for descoring and control zone coverage. When the chamber moves to the down position, the catch releases and the wing swings out of the way, so it doesn't block the chamber hole or interfere with scoring.

This means the wing deployment is essentially tied to the chamber state, wing out when we're not actively scoring, wing tucked when we are. This is a nice side effect because you generally want to descore or claim control zone when you're not in the middle of a scoring cycle anyway.

docs.title: Build:
docs.text: The wing and pivot mechanism is currently in the prototype stage. We have the basic pivot mounted and are testing the one-way catch engagement with the chamber linkage. The notebook deadline came before we could finish building and refining the final version.

docs.title: Test:
docs.text: Testing is pending, the prototype needs to be completed before we can run proper tests on descoring effectiveness and control zone coverage. This is a priority for after the notebook submission.

docs.title: Identify:
docs.text: A PTO is a "power take off" where you have some sort of mechanism/gearshift that switches a motor between two (or more applications)

docs.title: Why do we need a PTO?
docs.text:
In our last bot we were very fast, to achieve that (without overheating) we needed a 6 motor drive, this was very limiting on the other mechanisms on our bot because we only had 2 more motors we could use.

A PTO can help solve this problem; we don't always need the torque of all 6 motors, so when we don't need them on the drive train we can switch 2 motor off and use them in other mechanisms. This would be especially useful for mechanism's that could use energy stored in elastics/similar (ex. like theorized in Linear Scoring)

Timeline of PTO: Use stored energy is used --> PTO switches 2 motors off the drive train --> those 2 motors wind up the stored energy --> the energy is used --> repeat.

Even if we aren't going to store energy is is still very viable

docs.title: Brainstorm:
docs.text:
How would we actuality accomplish this? There are 2 main ways of implementing a PTO:

Vertically: This method rotates the motor gear around a pivot point to mesh with a top or bottom gear: Image Credit

Horizontally: This method slides the motor gear along a shaft and slides to the teeth of one gear or another, I can't find a very good example of this method for a PTO but this one is a transmission and the concept is the same:

Image Credit: I can't' find where I got this from...

This particular one uses two "fingers" to move the gears side to side and engage different gears.

docs.title: Pros:
docs.text:
• Very fast switching
  • Relatively simple

docs.title: Cons:
docs.text:
• If enough pressure isn't applied it can skip teeth under high load
  • Requires a lot of vertical space

docs.title: Pros:
docs.text:
• Loses no torque
  • Very reliable when tuned

docs.title: Cons:
docs.text:
• Not super fast switching
  • A bit more complicated
  • More friction

docs.text: I am going to select the horizontal method because the chance of running out of air is not worth it to me, because if we ran out of air for the vertical method, we wouldn't be able to use it in ether application (drivetrain/other).

docs.title: Problem:
docs.text: Our current bot can be pushed around more than I would like, we need a way to fix that.

docs.title: Brainstorm:
docs.text:
We need more traction and torque, mostly traction, as we cant really change torque as the speed is set in mostly dry clay.

Because speed (and torque is set) we need other solutions to help with pushing/being pushed. Something that could help is adding angled skirts to edge of the drivetrain

As shown in this diagram, if we have a slope on the edge of our bot if another bot tries to push us it would get lifted up losing the majority of its traction This also helps with pushing other bots, because when we go push someone else it will lift them up a little bit , making them lose their traction and pushing us into the ground giving us more traction (we might have a little bit of a hard time with traction because we are planning on making our robot light)

There is a problem with this however; to be most effective the skirts bust be close to the ground, and that will make it difficult to park, so we need a way to raise up the skirt, and if we add that ability, we might as well make it so we can push it into the ground making effectively immovable This can also help with Parking; we could make it the same mechanism.

docs.title: Legality:
docs.text:
Rule GG17 states that a Robot may not Hold an opposing Robot for more than a 3-count during the Driver Controlled Period.

Holding is defined as:

Holding - A Robot status; see rule < GG17 > for more information. Holding is legal until it exceeds the limits in < GG17 >. A Robot is considered to be Holding if it meets any of the following criteria during a Match: - Trapping - Limiting the movement of an opponent Robot to a small or confined area of the Field, approximately the size of one foam field tile or less, without an avenue for escape. Note that if a Robot is not attempting to escape, it is not considered Trapped. - Pinning - Preventing the movement of an opponent Robot through contact with the Field Perimeter, a Field Element, or another Robot. - Lifting - Controlling an opponent’s movements by raising or tilting the opponent’s Robot off of the foam tiles. Preventing a Robot that is already off of the Floor from returning to the Floor may also be considered Lifting or Trapping.

It is also mentioned that "Holding is a standard and legal part of Head-to-Head game play, and only becomes a Violation if it exceeds the guidelines in this rule. By beginning a Holding count immediately after noticing a Holding interaction, and providing a visual signal when a Holding interaction has been cleared, Head Referees can help Teams avoid penalties."

Therefore if we were to use a skirt/wedge to lift another robot it would just be considered Holding and is not directly illegal.

docs.title: Identify:
docs.text: We need a good reliable intake.

docs.title: Constraints:
docs.text:
• No jamming
  • Quick
  • Work with color sorting
  • Light
  • Not get tangled
  • Get blocks from wall well

docs.title: Rubber band intake
docs.text: This intake type uses sprockets and rubber bands to make a spinning drum that intakes the blocks.

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• Simple
  • Little required tuning
  • Can be static (not move up and down)
  • Doesn't rely solely on friction, the gaps in the rubber bands act as little "slots" for the blocks to go into.

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• Tangles with other robots easily
  • Rubber bands break and it goes through a lot of them
  • Jams if not done right (block can get stuck against the sprockets)

docs.title: Flex wheel intake
docs.text: This intake type uses a line of flex-wheels to grip the blocks and intake them Credit

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• No constant replacements needed
  • Generally smaller than a rubber band intake
  • Harder to jam

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• Once the flex wheels get dirty/dusty it barely works
  • Need to be mounted on a pivot (move up and down)

docs.title: Chain flap intake
docs.text: This intake method uses sprockets with rubber-flap chains like so:

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• Doesn't need replacing
  • Doesn't matter if it is dirty (doesn't rely on friction to much)

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• Not as affective as rubber band or flex wheel intakes (when they are working well)
  • It is "floppy"
  • To be effective it needs to be big

docs.text: Criteria Weight Rubber Band Flex Wheel Chain Flap Rubber Band Weighted Flex Wheel Weighted Chain Flap Weighted No jamming 5 3 4 4 15 20 20 Quick intake 3 4 4 2 12 12 6 Works with color sorting 3 2 4.5 2 6 13.5 6 Lightweight 2 4.5 2 3 9 4 6 Doesn't tangle 4 0 4 3.5 0 16 14 Gets blocks from wall 3 2.5 3 4 7.5 9 12 Low maintenance 2 2 3 5 4 6 10 Consistent 5 4 3 1 20 15 5 Weighted Total 73.5 95.5 79

docs.title: Scoring Rationale
docs.text:
Rubber Band Intake: Strong on speed, wall pickup, and consistency. Loses points for tangling and high maintenance (constant band replacements).

Flex Wheel Intake: Works well with color sorting, quick, and doesn't tangle. Penalized for dust sensitivity and requiring a pivot mechanism.

Chain Flap Intake: Lowest maintenance. Main weaknesses are is its consistency, size, and mediocrity on everything else.

docs.text: Flex wheel intake

docs.title: Repeat:
docs.text: (But more specific this time)

docs.title: Identify:
docs.text: We have chosen to use a flex wheel intake, but there are more specific things that we need to decide: - Size of flex wheel - Height of flex wheels - Y position of flex wheels - Speed of intake - How to pivot intake - How to power intake - How wide to make the intake - Spacing of flex wheels

docs.title: Size of flex wheel
docs.text: 1.625" or 2" 2" because it has more "squish" (give) than the 1.625" and that helps with grip and not needing to pivot as much.

docs.title: Height of flex wheels
docs.text: The flex wheels will have a absolute maximum distance from the ground of 3.25" because that is the smallest distance between any 2 opposite points on a block ~3.8" I think that we should have a minimum distance (and normal position) of 3.125 as the 0.125" adds a bit of grip to the intake. We also need the intake to be able to move up at least 0.55" up with the pivot

docs.title: Y position of flex wheels
docs.text: How far forward we want the intake. We need to stay in size, and we don't have much wiggle room, so the question is do we put it where it is in the image, or 0.5" forward: Where it is in the image is probably better because that makes it so we can have a match-loader aligner on the front.

docs.title: Speed of intake
docs.text:
Our bot can move at ~70in/s so it would be ideal to have the intake have a radial speed of 70in/s as well, for that we need a rpm of: $$ \pi \cdot d = \pi \cdot 2\text{ in} = 6.28\text{ in/rotation} $$ $$ \text{RPM} = \frac{70\text{ in}}{\text{ sec}} \cdot \frac{60\text{sec}}{\text{min}} \cdot \frac{\text{rotation}}{6.28\text{ in}}= $$ $$ \text{RPM} = \frac{70\cancel{\text{ in}}}{\cancel{\text{ sec}}} \cdot \frac{60\cancel{\text{sec}}}{\text{min}} \cdot \frac{\text{rotation}}{6.28\cancel{\text{ in}}}= \frac{4200\text{ rotation}}{6.28\text{ min}}= 668.78 \text{ RPM} $$

So, it looks like 600 RPM would be a good speed.

docs.title: Match-load theoretical max speed
docs.text:
Zach wants to be able intake blocks as fast as they fall from a match-load tube. The tube has 6 blocks but one is already on the ground, so 5 blocks fall. Each block is 3.25" tall when stacked, and we'll treat them as spheres with diameter 3.625".

Time for each block to fall: Using \(h = \frac{1}{2}gt^2\) and solving for \(t = \sqrt{\frac{2h}{g}}\) with \(g = 386.1\text{ in/s}^2\) (\(9.8\text{ m/s}^2\)):

Block Fall Height Time to ground 1 0" 0s 2 3.25" 0.130s 3 6.5" 0.183s 4 9.75" 0.225s 5 13" 0.259s 6 16.25" 0.290s

The shortest gap between blocks is between block 5 and 6: \(0.290 - 0.259 = 0.031\text{s}\)

To intake a 3.625" block in 0.031s: $$ \text{Speed} = \frac{3.625\text{ in}}{0.031\text{ s}} = 117\text{ in/s} $$

Converting to RPM with 2" flex wheels: $$ \text{RPM} = \frac{117\text{ in}}{\text{sec}} \cdot \frac{60\text{ sec}}{\text{min}} \cdot \frac{\text{rotation}}{6.28\text{ in}}= $$ $$ \text{RPM} = \frac{117\cancel{\text{ in}}}{\cancel{\text{sec}}} \cdot \frac{60\cancel{\text{ sec}}}{\text{min}} \cdot \frac{\text{rotation}}{6.28\cancel{\text{ in}}}= \frac{7020\text{ rotation}}{6.28\text{ min}}= 1118\text{ RPM} $$

This theoretical max of 1118 RPM is faster than a blue motor (600 RPM). However, this assumes each block must be fully intaked before the next arrives. In practice, blocks can queue on the intake, so 600 RPM should still work for match-loading.

Time to clear a match-load tube: The last block hits the ground at 0.290s. After that, we need to intake 6 blocks at 600 RPM (70 in/s): $$ \text{Intake time} = \frac{6\text{ blocks} \cdot 3.625\text{ in/block}}{70\text{ in/s}} = \frac{21.75\text{ in}}{70\text{ in/s}} = 0.311\text{ s} $$

Total time to clear a match-load tube: $$ \text{Total} = 0.290\text{ s (falling)} + 0.311\text{ s (intaking)} = 0.601\text{ s} \approx \textbf{0.6 seconds} $$ Therefore (ahem... Zach) at 600 RPM we could theoretically clear a match-load tube in 0.6 seconds

docs.title: Problems with Old Scoring (and Intake):
docs.text:
Our past bot used rollers to pull blocks from the basket and score them. This method worked decently well and was able to move a lot of blocks pretty quickly. But had some issues:

  1. Rubber band entanglement - The intake (and output) relied on rubber bands, which were really good at intaking but would get entangled with other bots. This would either:
    • Break the rubber bands completely
    • Make our bot stuck to the opponent for the rest of the match
  2. Jamming when overheated - The system would jam if the motors got too hot during extended use
  3. Size - The system was almost or more than half the bot and we couldn't fit under the goal
  4. Middle/Bottom goal - The old system could barely score in the middle goal if at all, and could only really score one block at a time in the bottom goal.

docs.title: What Worked Well:
docs.text:
• Fast block movement
  • Effective intake (when not entangled)
  • Generally consistent performance under normal conditions

docs.title: Goals for New Scoring System:
docs.text:
• Extremely fast scoring capability
  • More reliable (jamming)
  • No overheating issues under full match load
  • Ability to score specific quantities of blocks (important for autonomous)
  • Color sorting capability for strategic play
  • Fit under long goal

docs.title: Research - Current Meta:
docs.text:
Looking at top-performing bots at competitions, we've identified several effective scoring mechanisms:

  1. Basket - What we used before, moderate speed
  2. Lever - Currently the fastest method (6 blocks in ~0.5 seconds)
  3. S-bot -
  4. C-bot -

docs.title: Dual-Chamber Idea:
docs.text: Regardless of which mechanism we choose, we're considering using 2 scoring chambers side-by-side that converge into one output point. But there are multiple way to push the blocks: - Arc Scoring - Linear Scoring

docs.title: Potential Advantages:
docs.text:
• ~12 block capacity (double the standard 6)
  • Color sorting - one color per chamber
  • Strategic flexibility - can score from either chamber independently
  • Redundancy - if one jams, we can still use the other
  • Very fast - SPEED

docs.title: Scoring Methods Under Consideration:
docs.text:
1. Arc Scoring - Arc/lever mechanism analysis
  2. Linear Scoring - Linear elastic-powered system
  3. S Scoring - S-shaped path variation
  4. C Scoring - C-shaped path variation

docs.title: Select:
docs.text: Based on the ideas discussed in the above sections; the best option looks to be an Arc-Scoring lever as it: - Utilizes the PTO more effectively than linear options - Can fit 12 blocks (double standard capacity with dual chamber) - Doesn't have cooldown between uses.

docs.title: C Scoring
docs.text: Edit History Daren: 100.0% DateAuthor 2026-02-16Daren

docs.title: Overview:
docs.text: C-scoring uses a C-shaped path where blocks are loaded in from one side and scored out the other, following a curved channel. This is similar to S-scoring but with a different geometry.

docs.title: Why We Didn't Choose This:
docs.text:
Like S-scoring, the main problem with C-scoring is that it doesn't lend itself well to color sorting. The continuous curved path doesn't give you a natural point to eject or redirect blocks of the wrong color. You'd need some kind of gate or diverter mid-path, which adds complexity and failure points.

Since we believe color sorting is essential to our strategy, especially for skills autonomous where you need to only score your own color, a C-bot design doesn't fit our needs. The arc-scoring lever approach gives us much better control over individual blocks and works naturally with our dual-chamber color sorting system.

See Color Sorting for more on why we prioritize this capability, and Arc Scoring for the approach we selected instead.

docs.title: S Scoring
docs.text: Edit History Daren: 100.0% DateAuthor 2026-02-16Daren

docs.title: Overview:
docs.text: S-scoring uses an S-shaped path to guide blocks from the intake to the goal. The blocks follow a curved channel and are pushed through by rollers or a conveyor-style mechanism.

docs.title: Why We Didn't Choose This:
docs.text:
The biggest issue with S-scoring is that it makes color sorting extremely difficult. Because the blocks are traveling along a fixed, curved path, there's no good point to divert a block of the wrong color without completely disrupting the flow. You'd essentially have to stop the whole system to reject a block, which kills your cycle time.

We think color sorting is one of the most important capabilities for our bot, it lets us run dual chambers (one color per side), which is critical for skills autonomous and for not accidentally scoring the opponent's color. An S-bot design would force us to either give up color sorting or add a lot of complexity to make it work, neither of which is a good tradeoff.

See Color Sorting for more on why we prioritize this capability.

docs.title: Size and shape
docs.text: In order for us to fit 6 (12 total) in a chamber we will want to look at how much liner space we need: A block has a maximum size of ~4 inches if we plan for worst case we would need (6*4=) 24 inches of chamber (worst case) If we look at the smallest distance (3.25 inches) we will need a minimum of 19.5 inches. Therefore, to fit 6 blocks we need the chamber(s) to have a 19.5-24 inch path length I drew out the design with some constraints, and there is a little problem: With the current constraints the easiest spot for the chambers to go is not long enough (understatement). With a path length of 17 inches the most blocks we could fit would be ~5.2 blocks which is useable.

docs.title: Chamber height
docs.text: We need to think about how we are going to change heights as we think about size. The most common (and easiest) way to do this is a four bar lift to switch between the long and mid goal:

docs.title: Levers
docs.text:
We need a way to push the blocks out the front of the lever. My first idea is to use a pivoting c-channel (commonly used for lever bots) like this: It pivots up and pushes the blocks There is a little problem with this; the position of where it would need to pivot is really far forward and the way the PTO is setup right now is not ideal for this: It would be ideal to just use this pivot point, and i have an idea on how to do so. 4-bar lever: A 4-bar lift that has the horizontal bars attached on opposite sides to allow 180° of motion with a pushing "head" that stays facing one direction at all times. This has a great advantage as it lets us put the pivot point in the middle of the chamber as opposed to the front of the chamber. With this exact mechanism has a few problems with the angle of how it pushes the blocks (it would likely get stuck). A solution to this is to use a trapezoidal four-bar linkage instead of a normal 2 bar linkage where the top and bottom links are different lengths. this causes the angle of the "head" to rotate as it pivots. After messing around with different spacing i found one that works really well:

With this motion the blocks shouldn't get stuck as easily

After thinking about the integration with the color sorting and the intake this needs to be a lot more precise than "mess around until we find one that works" so i need to learn how Four-bar linkages work.

I have come up with a new motion for the lever: This mechanical wonder of a creation is very simple in execution, but took a long time to get it tweaked just right. It works so well because in the resting position it is perfectly folded out of the way: We will likely design the chamber around the lever path because the required precision to change the path is in like 0.01" increments and the holes are every 0.5" so this is the closest we are gonna get.

docs.title: Speed
docs.text:
We need to figure out what speed we need the lever to rotate, Zach wants to be able to score 5 (or 6) blocks in 500ms. The lever has to rotate a quarter turn to score all the blocks in the chamber, and we have an input from the PTO of 200RPM (blue motor geared 3:1)

Target RPM: $$ \text{RPM} = \frac{0.25\text{ rotations}}{0.5\text{ sec}} \cdot \frac{60\text{ sec}}{\text{min}} = $$ $$ \text{RPM} = \frac{0.25\text{ rotations}}{0.5\cancel{\text{ sec}}} \cdot \frac{60\cancel{\text{ sec}}}{1\text{ min}} = \frac{15\text{ rotations}}{0.5\text{ min}} = 30 \text{ RPM} $$ Input RPM → Target RPM: Because our input RPM is the same as a green motor (200 RPM) we can just steal the table from the drivetrain-speed

RPM 1:1 5:6 4:5 3:4 2:3 3:5 1:2 2:5 1:3 1:4 1:5 1:6 1:7 200 200 166.7 160 150 133.3 120 100 80 66.7 50 40 33.3 28.6

We can see the closest gear ratio to this is a 1:6 ratio (12:72) that gives us 33.3 RPM which is definitely close enough.

Using this gear ratio has its own problems though, because the high torque multiplication could cause the gears to slip if not mounted well

docs.title: Torque
docs.text:
We need to make sure an 11W motor can push the blocks with a 12" lever arm.

Motor torque at 1:6 gear ratio: An 11W motor has a stall torque of ~1.67 N·m. With our 1:6 gear ratio: $$ \text{Output Torque} = \text{Motor Torque} \cdot \text{Gear Ratio} = 1.67\text{ N·m} \cdot 6 = 10.02\text{ N·m} $$

Converting to inch-pounds: $$ \text{Output Torque} = 10.02\text{ N·m} \cdot \frac{8.851\text{ in·lb}}{1\text{ N·m}} = 88.7\text{ in·lb} $$

Force at end of 12" lever: $$ \text{Force} = \frac{\text{Torque}}{\text{Lever Length}} = \frac{88.7\text{ in·lb}}{12\text{ in}} = 7.39\text{ lb} $$

Converting to Newtons: $$ \text{Force} = 7.39\text{ lb} \cdot \frac{4.448\text{ N}}{1\text{ lb}} = 32.9\text{ N} $$

So at stall, the lever can push with approximately 7.4 lbs (32.9 N) of force at the end of the 12" arm.

With this gear ratio looking at the lever placement vs the PTO input; it's kinda not in a good placement: I was able to move the PTO output by flipping the motor around and everything else too. This makes the position much better for the lever gear:

docs.title: Arc Scoring
docs.text: Arc scoring is using a lever to push blocks along an arc-shaped path and into the goals.

docs.title: How It Works:
docs.text: The way this would work is by using a PTO (Power Take Off) to switch 2 of the drivetrain motors to the lever(s), and rotate them along the arc, which would be full of blocks. This method has been proven to be able to score 6 blocks in 1/2 a second. This method of scoring is also known to jam a lot if it's not built properly.

docs.title: Pros:
docs.text:
• Is extremely fast
  • Can score a specific amount of blocks (1, 2, 3, etc.) - this is important for things like autonomous period and skills autonomous, when you want to only score one or 2 blocks, and not everything you are holding
  • Can have variable speed, in case you want to launch the blocks really hard and fast to either de-score, or try and win a pushing match where there's 2 bots on opposing ends of goals just holding it, or if you want to score slowly to not shoot them through the middle goal
  • Very lightweight

docs.title: Cons:
docs.text:
• Can be weak if it's not built for torque
  • Takes up more room than linear (harder to go under goals)
  • Can have issues with intaking if not built correctly
  • 4 motor drive while scoring

docs.title: Conclusion:
docs.text:
I think this is the better method of scoring due to the fact that linear isn't adjustable. Like it can't vary the speed, or the amount of blocks it scores, it's all or nothing. With the lever arm, you can do just about anything in terms of scoring. You can make it super slow to score, or you can make it launch the blocks out the other side of the long goal.

For auton, you can score one or two in the middle, and the rest in the long goal. Or if you want to get AWP, you can score 1 in the middle goal, go to match loader and score 2 in the long goal, then go to the other match loader and score all 6 into the other long goal, and use a wing to get control zone. This gives an insane head start to the rest of the match, with us already owning one goal.

docs.title: Brainstorm:
docs.text:
One way to score blocks is using a linear mechanism to push the blocks. My idea is a little difficult to describe in words so here is a diagram:

In the block chamber we have a liner rail and slide and on that slide we have something to push the blocks out the end. The slide would have elastic string attached to it that would be wound up by the PTO.

There would be 3 main states:

State 1: In this state there is no tension on the elastic string or the block pusher thingy, but the latch holds the block pusher thingy from going forward.

State 2: State 2 is vary similar to state 2 except that the PTO has wound up the elastic string and stored the energy to be released by the latch

State 3: State 3 is the same as state 2 but after the latch has been released but the string is still wound up.

After state 3 the PTO unwinds the elastic string and a small elastic pulls the slide back into the latch resetting to state 1

docs.title: Pros:
docs.text:
• Doesn't take up a lot of additional space
  • Doesn't require a motor to actively use (to score blocks)
  • Can release a lot more energy at once than a motor directly (it just takes time to wind up, the limit isn't torque it's time)
  • Is extremely fast at scoring
  • can be very lightweight

docs.title: Cons:
docs.text:
• Less efficient block storage (not curved)
  • A bit complicated (ok, maybe a lot)
  • Not super controllable
  • Requires the PTO to be engaged in winding mode for much longer time than other methods would require
  • difficult (if not impossible) to score less than all of the blocks in the chamber

docs.title: Top Funnel
docs.text: Edit History Daren: 100.0% DateAuthor 2026-02-16Daren

docs.title: Identify:
docs.text: Our dual-chamber scoring system has two separate chambers side by side, but the goal opening is only one chamber wide. and we don't want to have to move over to score the other chamber. We need a way to funnel both chambers into a single output point so blocks from either chamber can score into the same goal.

docs.title: Constraints:
docs.text:
• Size Must not make the bot any bigger than it already is before expansion. The funnel has to fold or tuck within our existing footprint.
  • Block retention Must keep blocks contained and not let them fall out during movement or scoring.

docs.title: Brainstorm:
docs.text:
There's really only one approach that isn't immediately rejected: folding plastic pieces driven by a pneumatic. The funnel is made of 4 pieces: the top and bottom are regular 45-degree trapezoids that angle inward, and the two side pieces are mostly square. When all four unfold, they form a square hole the size of one chamber opening at the front, funneling both chambers into one output. When retracted, all four pieces fold flat against the chambers.

Other ideas like fixed funnels or rigid converging walls were rejected because they'd push us over size limits or permanently block one chamber.

docs.title: Select:
docs.text: We went with the pneumatic-driven folding funnel. When the pneumatic fires, the four pieces unfold, trapezoids on top and bottom angle inward, square sides close in, forming a square opening that aligns with the goal. When retracted, they fold flat so we stay within size.
